content: The prevalence of hypertension has increased in the United States, partly due to the adoption of a lower diagnostic threshold of ≥130/80 mmHg, as recommended by the 2017 ACC/AHA guidelines, compared to the previous threshold of 140/90 mmHg. Globally, hypertension is a leading cause of mortality. Alarmingly, more than half of individuals with hypertension are unaware of their condition, and many diagnosed patients fail to adhere to prescribed treatments. Between 1910 and 1914, the terms essential hypertension and malignant hypertension were introduced to describe different forms of the condition. Hypertension is classified into two main categories: primary (essential) hypertension and secondary hypertension. Secondary hypertension, which accounts for 5% of cases, is caused by underlying medical conditions such as pheochromocytoma, obstructive sleep apnea, chronic kidney disease, hyperthyroidism, or Cushing syndrome. It may also result from certain medications or substance use, such as NSAIDs, alcohol, or stimulants like cocaine. Refractory hypertension is an even more severe form, unresponsive to at least five classes of antihypertensive drugs. The pathophysiology of hypertension involves complex mechanisms, including dysregulation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), endothelial dysfunction, and overactivation of the sympathetic nervous system. Genetic factors also play a role, with hypertension being a polygenic disorder. Environmental factors such as obesity, high sodium intake, low potassium intake, and physical inactivity further contribute to its development. Hypertension is highly prevalent, affecting approximately 45,600 per 100,000 individuals worldwide. It is more common in older adults, males, and individuals of Black, Asian, or Hispanic descent. Risk factors include diabetes, dyslipidemia, obesity, low socioeconomic status, physical inactivity, and psychological stress. Resistant hypertension is more frequently observed in older adults, individuals with chronic kidney disease, and those of Black race. If left untreated, hypertension can lead to severe complications, including myocardial infarction, stroke, end-stage renal disease, and death. Approximately 33% of untreated hypertensive patients may experience cardiovascular events. The prognosis is poor without treatment, with a 10-year mortality rate of approximately 11%. Primary hypertension is often asymptomatic, while secondary hypertension may present with symptoms such as palpitations, headaches, sweating, abdominal pain, or muscle cramps. Physical examination findings in secondary hypertension may include arterial bruits, irregular pulses, abdominal masses, or skin changes such as violaceous striae or hirsutism. Laboratory tests for hypertension include fasting blood sugar, complete blood count, lipid profile, serum creatinine with eGFR, and electrolyte levels. Optional tests may include uric acid and urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio. Electrocardiography (ECG) can help identify left ventricular hypertrophy, while imaging studies such as chest X-rays, echocardiography, CT scans, or MRI may be used to assess complications or underlying causes. The primary treatment for hypertension involves lifestyle modifications and pharmacological therapy. First-line medications include calcium channel blockers, ACE inhibitors or ARBs, and thiazide-like diuretics. Beta-blockers are used in specific conditions such as angina or heart failure. Resistant hypertension may require additional medications such as spironolactone or hydralazine. In cases of secondary hypertension, surgical interventions may be necessary, such as repair of aortic coarctation or adrenalectomy for primary aldosteronism.
